scope: Three lesson decisions: clearer questions, plausible distractors and explanatory feedback. Correct answers, main quiz, rewards and progress rules unchanged.
reviewStatus: Offline editorial review against dated local lessons; independent Grade 5 review and live comparison pending

expected.decisionSituation: This is a fictional classroom investigation. A community has both a river route and a sea crossing. What should travellers check?
expected.decisionQuestion: Which choice best fits the evidence and ideas you explored?
decisionChoices: Whether their boat and each part of the route suit the journey
Only the color of the boat
Whether all rivers have the same depth
Whether planning can be skipped
expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Whether their boat and each part of the route suit the journey
expected.decisionExplanation: The Philippines is an archipelago. Water separates islands but also provides routes between them. Boats could carry people, goods and messages. Rivers could connect inland places to the coast.

fields.decisionQuestion: What should the travellers check before choosing this river-and-sea journey?
decisionChoices: Whether their boat and each part of the route suit the journey
Whether the boat suits the river, without checking the sea crossing
Whether the route is short, without checking the boat
Whether another crew once used the route, without checking current conditions
fields.decisionExplanation: The journey includes both a river and a sea crossing. A boat suitable for one part may not suit the other. Check the boat, both parts of the route and current conditions. A short or previously used route does not by itself establish that the plan is suitable.

expected.decisionSituation: This is a fictional classroom investigation. A written account and an object suggest different details. What should researchers do?
expected.decisionQuestion: Which choice best fits the evidence and ideas you explored?
decisionChoices: Invent a third source
Compare the sources and explain what remains uncertain
Choose the prettier source
Hide the disagreement
expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Compare the sources and explain what remains uncertain
expected.decisionExplanation: Maps of past trade are explanations based on evidence. They are not photographs of every ship journey. Researchers use objects, written accounts and other sources together. Each source has limits.

fields.decisionQuestion: What should researchers do when these two sources suggest different details?
decisionChoices: Accept the written account because it names its author
Compare the sources and explain what remains uncertain
Accept the object alone because objects are from the past
Combine both details and report that the sources agree
fields.decisionExplanation: A written account and an object can provide different clues. Compare their dates, settings and what each can show. A named author or an old object is not enough to settle every question. Explain the disagreement instead of reporting agreement that the evidence does not show.

expected.decisionSituation: This is a fictional classroom investigation. A learner says a borrowed idea was accepted by everyone at once. What should they check?
expected.decisionQuestion: Which choice best fits the evidence and ideas you explored?
decisionChoices: The color of the map
Whether guesses can replace sources
Evidence of where, when and how people used it
Only whether the story sounds exciting
expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Evidence of where, when and how people used it
expected.decisionExplanation: People meeting through travel could share language, skills and beliefs. Cultural exchange can move in more than one direction. A community may change a borrowed idea to suit its needs. Not every group accepts the same ideas.

fields.decisionQuestion: What would help check whether people accepted the idea in different places and times?
decisionChoices: The number of similar objects, without checking when they were used
A map showing contact, without checking how people responded
Evidence of where, when and how people used it
One traveller's opinion, without comparing other people's experiences
fields.decisionExplanation: Contact gives people a chance to share an idea, but does not show that everyone accepted it at once. Compare evidence of its use in different places and times. Similar objects, a contact map or one opinion alone cannot establish how all people responded.
